10058606:
Written Testimony of Andrew Jura In Opposition to LD 2096 Submitted to the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry
To Senator Talbot-Ross, Representative Plueker, and members of the Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry Committee:
My name is Andrew Jura. I serve as First Vice President of the Union Fair, and I am a Maine small business owner. I have spent most of my working life in Maine's agricultural fairs--27 years as a vendor across the state, and the past three years working directly with the Union Fair.
To many people, a fair is just a weekend event. In Maine, however, a fair is something much deeper than that. It is where towns come together, where children see their first calf or chicken, where neighbors reconnect, where local nonprofits raise funds, and where small businesses earn the income they need to survive another year.
The Union Fair is not a recent tradition. It began in 1869 and has served its community for more than a century and a half. In that time, the fair has closed only during extraordinary moments in history--World War II and a worldwide pandemic. This year marks the Union Fair's 155th year. Its continuity reflects generations of volunteers, farmers, families, and community members who have worked tirelessly to preserve an institution deeply rooted in Maine's agricultural and cultural heritage.
This testimony is submitted in opposition to LD 2096.
As currently written, LD 2096 would change the definition of an agricultural fair in a way that does not reflect the realities of rural Maine. Many smaller fairs do not have the number of farms, exhibitors, volunteers, or financial resources available to larger fairs. If these changes are adopted, some of Maine's smaller fairs will not be able to continue operating.
Such an outcome would represent a loss not only for fairs, but for Maine communities.

Maine's agricultural landscape has changed. There are fewer farms than there once were, particularly in smaller towns. Yet fairs like the Union Fair have adapted. They continue to provide agricultural education through demonstrations, youth activities, and competitions that are realistic and sustainable within their communities. This work is carried out largely by volunteers, with limited budgets and significant commitment.
The Union Fair has long been part of its community's identity. It is where grandparents bring their grandchildren because they remember attending themselves. It is where residents who may not see one another throughout the year reconnect. It is where rural towns maintain a sense of shared identity and place.
A one-size-fits-all definition of an agricultural fair may appear orderly on paper, but it does not reflect the practical realities of Maine's diverse communities. If the state establishes standards that only larger fairs can meet, the result will not be a stronger agricultural system, but the gradual disappearance of smaller fairs that sustain rural community life.
When a fair disappears, the loss extends beyond the event itself. Opportunities for young people to learn about agriculture diminish. Local organizations lose important fundraising opportunities. Communities lose one of their most meaningful gathering places.
Every fair in Maine is different because every community in Maine is different. That diversity is not a weakness; it is a defining strength of Maine's agricultural tradition.
For these reasons, the committee is respectfully urged to reconsider LD 2096 and to preserve the current definition of an agricultural fair. Protecting Maine agriculture should not come at the cost of losing Maine's agricultural fairs and the communities they sustain.
Respectfully submitted,
Andrew Jura First Vice President, Union Fair
10058559:
Testimony of the Maine Organic Farmers and Gardeners Association in opposition of LD 2096 - An Act Regarding Scheduling of Agricultural Fairs
and Pulling
January 27, 2026
Good afternoon Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Committee. My name is April Boucher and I'm the Director for the Common Ground Country Fair, which is hosted by the Maine Organic Farmers and Gardeners Association (MOFGA). MOFGA appreciates the opportunity to testify in opposition of LD 2096, An Act Regarding Scheduling of Agricultural Fairs and Pulling, specifically lines 11-26 on page 1 of the bill, Sec.1. MRSA 81, sub-1.
The agricultural fairs of Maine have been successfully supporting and serving their local, and wider communities, for many years, and in some cases for over 200 years. Each Fair is unique and a true celebration of their area's agriculture and community.
As a result, we need to meet Fair's where they are and lift them up with support. The revised agricultural fair definition proposed would put undue hardship, and may even cause the closure, of some of our small and medium sized fairs.
The proposed revised definition also doesn't emphasize education, which is an integral part of our agricultural fairs. Last year 64,420 fairgoers attended the Common Ground Country Fair to avail themselves of over 600 educational opportunities and almost 50 family friendly activities. People keep coming back because we are investing in them, their families, and our communities.
Our Fairs also operate largely because of the skills and hard work of volunteers. For many volunteers, it is hard to take time off from work and many use their vacation time to help make fairs happen. It is also a challenge for farmers to be away from their farms for extended periods of time to exhibit and compete. We should not be `cancelling' a fair because their volunteers or exhibitors can only be away from their lives for a day or two. We need to meet our Fairs, volunteers, farmers, and exhibitors where they are and lift them up with support.

Thank you and I am happy to answer any questions.
___________________________________________________________________ About MOFGA: A broad-based community, MOFGA is transforming our food system by supporting farmers, empowering people to feed their communities, and advocating for an organic future. MOFGA certifies 537 organic farms and processing operations representing more than $120 million in sales. We're working hard to create opportunities for Maine's next generation of farmers. Each of these farmers is a Maine businessperson for whom economic health and environmental health are interdependent. While MOFGA envisions a future of healthy ecosystems, communities; people, and economies sustained by the practices of organic agriculture, we attribute our success to collaboration and outreach to growers across the management spectrum.

Testimony of Rep. Christina Mitchell introducing
LD 2096, An Act Regarding Scheduling of Agricultural Fairs and Pulling
Events Before the Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry Committee
Good afternoon, Senator Talbot-Ross, Representative Pluecker and distinguished members of the
Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry Committee. I am Christina Mitchell, and I represent the communities of Cumberland, Long Island and Chebeague Island. I am here today to introduce
LD 2096, An Act to Regarding Scheduling of Agricultural Fairs and Pulling Events.

The intent of LD 2096 is to address the concerns that arose with the fair dates last season
between two fairs. With this bill, I want to prevent what happened from recurring and from spreading to other fairs, especially smaller ones where the damage would be more harmful. I have an amendment to offer as well that focuses on this intent and does not go deep into
definition changes of an agricultural fair.

The situation that calls for the bill: the final day of any given fair in Maine is universally the
largest revenue-producing day. If a fair, as occurred last season, unilaterally steps into another fair's approved, licensed final dates, it causes financial, organizational and public confusion.
Fairs already operate on a very thin margin; to lose revenue from ticket sales, vendors and events is damaging to any fair in Maine. In our situation, it was confusing to the vendors and the public, as well as disruptive to the participants in the exhibits, competitions and Show events.

The solution: this bill provides the Commissioner of the Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry with tools to address any deviations from operating an agricultural fair outside its approved, licensed fair dates. Specifically, the bill provides that the Commissioner
may suspend or revoke the license of a licensee that is in violation of the provisions in the bill.
The bill also provides that a scheduled public or private pulling event must take place during the dates of the fair's license and specifies that a pulling event that is not conducted in accordance

with this provision is not entitled to a stipend.

-

There are fair officials present that can speak directly to the impact of the fair date overlap last
fair season. I understand that many fairs beyond the one in my district are very concerned about

District 110: Chebeague Island, Cumberland and Long Island

facing a similar situation. This bill provides the Commissioner of ACF the tools and authority
needed to address and prevent such an occurrence from happening again.
Thank you for your time and consideration. I am happy to answer any questions, but I would defer specifics to the fair officials who are with us today.
District 110: Chebeague Island, Cumberland and Long Island
10058762:
David Andrews
Fryeburg Fair, General Superintendent Email: dandrews@fryeburgfair.org Phone: 207.935.3268
Testimony LD 2096
January 27, 2026
Good afternoon esteemed members of the committee, thank you for the opportunity to address you today. My name is David Andrews, I am the General Superintendent at Fryeburg Fair.
Maine has fairs of all sizes; we have common goals to promote agriculture and create community events in our state. As our industry changes, we as fairs must change or we will be left behind.
After consulting with a representative of the Department of Agriculture, Fryeburg Fair added the first Saturday. That extra day is the focus of this bill. We added this day because for years, many of our vendors have asked us to add Saturday. Those vendors include approximately 40 non-profit, civic organizations who make most of their operating revenue during the fair. This extra day affords the Fair some rain insurance as our large overhead does not diminish during rain events but our revenue suffers greatly.
Some in the fair industry still believe that there are two segments to their fair, the carnival and the fair. Carnivals and fairs should be partners working together because without a carnival and all they bring with them, food venders, rides and shopping, most fairs would be hard pressed to cover the overhead of operating.
Before 2017, the United States had more than 400 carnival operators. We have lost more than half of the carnivals which now total about 170 operators. This would indicate to me that the remaining carnivals will at some point start to pick and choose the fairs that offer the best business opportunities for them. The fairs that operate Sunday to Saturday may want to consider filling those weekend dates as the Sunday to Saturday dates are becoming less desirable for carnivals because of the loss of a whole weekend. Fairs at some point may be asked to renegotiate their carnival dates.
Maine fairs are already at a disadvantage because of our Geographic location. I have asked carnivals at the National Conference if they would be interested in coming to Maine to operate. Due to the cost and travel time associated with our location as well as incomplete weekends, those that were asked could not accommodate Maine.
I am opposed to LD 2096. Maine fairs need the flexibility to adjust, add or reduce dates as needed as long as they are fulfilling their missions.
I am asking you to kill this bill as it will have a negative impact on fairs, and create barriers that will hinder the prosperity and ability to change as the industry changes.
Thank you for your time.
David Andrews
10058442:
25 January 2026
To the Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry Committee I write asking you to strike line 5 and lines 11-26 from this proposed legislation.
Changing the definition of Agriculture fairs in the State of Maine will have a detrimental impact on 24% of the total number of fairs in Maine resulting in a significant loss to the local and state economy.
Line 26, which requires at least three consecutive days of operation, will immediately close two fairs in rural communities as they offer competition on only two days.
Lines 20-23 could result in the closure of four other rural fairs that have been running for decades in their communities.
According to the 2025 IAFE Economic Impact Survey, these small, rural fairs generate $107,336 state tax dollars EACH with an average economic impact of $4,291,617 in their communities. On average each of these fairs supports 31 jobs and generates $1,452,804 in annual wages in their communities.
The text change proposed in lines 20-26 will have an adverse impact on Maine communities. The loss of these fairs would remove $25,749,702 in economic activity from rural areas. This text will effectively cost 186 jobs across these communities along with approximately $650,000 in state tax revenue.
It will result in loss of funds local groups raise each year at the fair to support their community activities. Any local tax generated by these fairs will be lost.
These 61 words of text will cause a financial impact felt in these communities along with the loss of years of dedicated work by generations of Mainers. I am hoping that my testimony is sharing an unintended consequence of well-meaning legislation and not shining a light on a misguided attempt to close fairs in the smallest communities because they somehow don't represent someone's ideal of what an agriculture fair should be.
All of Maine's fairs together contribute not just to the state economy, but to the preservation of things uniquely Maine and to the celebration of the present and future of Maine agriculture.
I plead with you NOT to change the definition of agriculture fair as part of this legislation. Let it be legislation that supports fairs, not kills a quarter of all fairs in the state.
Sincerely,
David Grindle President and CEO
10058484:
Testimony of Fryeburg Fair
In opposition to LD 2096, An Act Regarding Scheduling of Agricultural Fairs and Pulling Events
Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker and Members of the Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, I am David Hastings, President of the West Oxford Agricultural Society which operates the Fryeburg Fair and I come before you today to testify in opposition to LD 2096.
This bill makes dramatic changes to the statutes governing Maine's Agricultural Fairs. It will have the effect of disqualifying several of our smallest fairs from the right to share in the Fair Stipend Fund which may put them out of business. It also will establish the requirement that fairs obtain a license just to operate, which has never been required in Maine.
It is our understanding that this bill is submitted on behalf of the Cumberland Fair. It is not a department bill and was written without any consultation or input of the impacted stakeholders such as the Maine Association of Agricultural Fairs or any of the other 20 plus existing Agricultural Fairs.
We oppose Section 1 of the bill which establishes an entirely new definition of an Agricultural Fair. According to the Maine Association of Agricultural Fairs, it appears that this new definition will disqualify a number of our smaller fairs from operating as an Agricultural Fair in the future and deny them any access to the Fair's Stipend Fund. I have no idea why the sponsor would wish to eliminate any of our smaller fairs.
We strongly oppose Sections 2 through 7 of the bill which will also make a dramatic change in the law without input from stakeholders. Maine's Agricultural Fairs have never been required to obtain a license to operate. The existing statutes only require fairs to seek licensed dates from the Department of Agriculture,
1

Conservation and Forestry if they want to participate in the Fair Stipend Fund which uses casino revenues to reimburse Fairs for a portion of premiums paid for competitions at their fairs.
If the Legislature is now going to require fairs to obtain a license just to operate, then the requirements for obtaining such a license need to be clearly spelled out. This proposed legislation only says that a license is required for an Agricultural Fair to operate, but does not list the requirements to obtain the license. Will small fairs which cannot meet the new definition of an Agricultural Fair be shut down? Without clear licensing requirements, how can it be determined if a license applicant was granted or denied a license properly, improperly or arbitrarily?
If such drastic changes in the laws regarding agricultural fairs are to be made, they should only be made after bringing together the stakeholders to participate and have input in the creation of the new licensing requirements. In this case, no input was obtained from any of the stakeholders as far as we can tell. The Maine Association of Agricultural Fairs was not consulted. No other individual fairs were consulted. The department was apparently was not consulted in any great detail.
This is not the proper way to enact legislation affecting an entire industry.
It is the belief of Fryeburg Fair that this legislation was brought forward solely at the request of Cumberland Fair which is unhappy with the decision of Fryeburg Fair, located 50 miles and an hour and ten minutes from Cumberland, to move its opening day from Sunday to Saturday, which overlaps with Cumberland's closing day. Overlapping fair dates are common. There are already more than a dozen instances of overlapping dates in Maine. It became apparent to Fryeburg Fair that makes no sense for fairs to leave weekend days unused. That is when the public can attend fairs. Cumberland and Fryeburg both had good days on that overlapping Saturday. Having now established this, Fryeburg is now applying to have its opening Saturday licensed under the existing statute for participation in the Stipend Fund.
For these reasons, Fryeburg Fair urges this Committee to vote ought not to pass on this legislation.

10058573:
Erik Fitch Blue Hill Fair LD 2096
My Name is Erik Fitch, and I am The General Manager of the Blue Hill Fair a Labor Day tradition since 1891. We are one of the 25 licensed agricultural fairs across this beautiful state,
I am making this testimony in opposition to LD 2096. Specifically, to Section 1 lines 11-26 and Section 5
As written, this bill could immensely change the agricultural fair world in all corners of Maine. For some, the ramification could be catastrophic. Some of the fairs that you have come to love and made memories at for entire lifetimes might not be there anymore.
Maine agricultural fairs mean everything to the state of Maine. They are woven into the history, our economy, and our way of life. Maine fairs are a way to connect the public to the very people who raise livestock, grow crops, and produce many of the foods we enjoy. For many Mainers especially children our fairs are the first place they ever see a dairy cow up close, learn where their food really comes from, or understand the hard work of the farmers.
Economically, fairs are critical to communities all across the state. Some of the hardest hit fairs due to this bill are in areas that are already having major financial uncertainties. The Washington County Fair in Pembroke is the newest fair in Maine and is open for two days in August. This fair according to a 2025 economic impact study by Johnson Consulting in partnership with the International Association of Fairs and Expos (IAFE) Washington County Fair had a $217,000 estimated fiscal impact in that area of the state. The Springfield Fair according to the same study referenced above had an estimated $790,000 fiscal impact in the rural setting in northern Penobscot County. Both of these fairs could be closed due to the ramifications of this bill.
In closing, we need to protect our Maine fairs at all cost. It one of the oldest traditions that can be enjoyed without the interference of a cell phone. Kids with smiles as big as a Ferris wheel. Grandparents reminiscing of their first date at the local fair with a large cotton candy. Let's keep these opportunities available for the next generation.
Thank you for your time
Erik Fitch Blue Hill Fair Blue Hill Maine

LD2096January 27, 2026 Good afternoon, Senator Talbot-Ross, Representative Plueker, and distinguished members of the Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry Committee.
My name is Mel Chadbourne. I am a Trustee of the Harmony Free Fair in Harmony, Maine, where I have served for 27 years in leadership roles, including Vice-president and multiple Trustee terms.
Today, I submit this testimony in opposition to LD 2096, specifically Section 1, Lines 11-26, and Section 5. Changing the definition of an "agricultural fair" is unnecessary and harmful. Maine's agricultural fairs have operated successfully under the current definition for decades. The proposed changes would fundamentally alter that framework and would disproportionately impact small, community-based fairs like the Harmony Free Fair.
The agricultural landscape in rural Maine has changed dramatically. In our region, there are no longer any 4-H groups, and the last remaining dairy farm closed just last year. What remains are primarily small, backyard farms. These individuals rely on the Harmony Free Fair for education, demonstrations, and connection to agricultural traditions. While we do offer some animal competitions, we do not have the local farm base, youth infrastructure, or resources to meet the requirements outlined in LD 2096 as currently proposed.
Mandating competitions across multiple livestock and poultry species is not feasible for fairs with limited exhibitor pools. Requiring three or more youth agriculture events would present an additional challenge. These requirements do not strengthen agricultural education; instead, they create barriers that many fairs cannot overcome. In practice, this legislation would force at least one of Maine's 25 agricultural fairs to close and could threaten the survival of many small-sized fairs statewide. In 2025, the Harmony Free Fair celebrated its 77th anniversary. Under the proposed redefinition, reaching our 78th year would be uncertain.
The Harmony Free Fair is more than an event--it is a deeply rooted community tradition. Families who have moved away plan their visits home around fair week. Neighbors reconnect. This past year, a mother brought her one-day-old baby to the fair, explaining that she had never missed one and did not intend to start now. The fair provides something increasingly rare: face-to-face connection in a world dominated by screens.
Friends and families gather to enjoy agricultural education, demonstrations, modest competitions, affordable local entertainment, and a strong sense of community. Each fair in Maine reflects the character and needs of its region. That diversity is not a weakness; it is the reason Maine's fairs endure.
Hundreds of volunteers dedicate their time and energy to preserving these fairs, which remain Maine's most accessible agricultural education entities. What we have works and redefining agricultural fairs in a way that excludes long-standing, successful models is unnecessary and damaging.
I am unable to attend today due to illness, but I welcome the opportunity to answer any questions. Thank you for your time, consideration, and continued support of Maine's 25 agricultural fairs.
Respectfully submitted,
Mary Ellen (Mel) Chadbourne Trustee, Harmony Free Fair

Testimony of Senator Teresa S. Pierce in support of LD 2096, An Act Regarding Scheduling of Agricultural Fairs and Pulling Events
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry
January 27, 2026
Good morning, Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and esteemed members of the Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry Committee. My name is Teresa Pierce. I represent Senate District 25, which includes Falmouth, Cumberland, North Yarmouth, most of Yarmouth, Gray and Long Island. I am also honored to serve as the Senate Assistant Majority Leader. I write to you in strong support of LD 2096.
The Cumberland Fair has been a staple of our community for 153 years, and this summer we will celebrate the 154th edition. For years, Agricultural Fairs, in consultation with the Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry have established schedules to ensure minimal overlap of these exciting annual fairs.
Unfortunately last summer, the longstanding agreements were not followed leaving the Cumberland Fair in unnecessary competition with another agricultural fair. This change caused much disruption with the early departure of livestock and participants in exhibitions, competitions, pulling events.
LD 2096 bill would provide the Commissioner tools to address any such repeat occurrence. In effect, all the fairs would be more secure, knowing their dates were firm and cannot be infringed upon by another fair. The Cumberland Fair welcomes residents and visitors alike from across Maine and beyond who contribute to the local agricultural economy.
I appreciate Representative Mitchell for leading on this issue, collaborating with fair organizers, farmers and community leaders in a good-faith effort to ensure these iconic fairs each have their own week for fairgoers to enjoy.
Thank you for the opportunity to weigh in on this important issue for my district. I encourage you to vote Ought to Pass on LD 2096.
